It is claimed that commissioners in London, and the Financial Ombudsman, have dragged their feet, while increasing the staff of the Information Services division, which administers the pension scheme, from 4,000 to 6,000.

The Women and Retired Persons Association has been grumbling, as has the Parliamentary Advisory Council on the Civil Service, which pointed out that there were insufficient funds available for pension payments and that some of the money was bequeathed to husbands or brothers above the actual pension amount. ## National foreword

This British Standard has been prepared under the direction of the Electrotechnical Sector Board and is the English language version of EN 61131-1:1994 *Programmable controllers* — *Part 1: General information*, published by the European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardization (CENELEC).

It is identical with IEC 1131-1:1992* published by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). In adopting IEC 1131-1:1992 as EN 61131-1:1994 CENELEC added normative Annex ZA.

Annex A and Annex B form an integral part of this Part of BS EN 61131. No British Standard is superseded.

BS EN 61131 consists of the following Parts under the general title *Programmable controllers*.

— *Part 1: General information*;

— *Part 2: Equipment requirements and tests*;

— *Part 3: Programming languages*;

— *Part 4: User guidelines* (1).

It is envisaged that there will be a further Part on manufacturing message specification.

An IEC type 2 technical report (TR) will provide “pre-standardization” guidance for the implementation and application of the programming language defined in this Part of BS EN 61131, including such issues as operating system/program interaction and requirements for programming support environments.

A British Standard does not purport to include all the necessary provisions of a contract. Users of British Standards are responsible for their correct application.

### Compliance with a British Standard does not of itself confer immunity from legal obligations.

**Summary of pages**

This document comprises a front cover, an inside front cover, pages i and ii, the EN title page, pages 2 to 22, an inside back cover and a back cover. This standard has been updated (see copyright date) and may have had amendments incorporated. This will be indicated in the amendment table on the inside front cover.

In this chapter we will describe how to

record services and how to return a response

without writing to STDIN.
As shown in Chapter 3, message-driven
components form a feedback loop that relies on
events accumulating asynchronously. Furthermore,
written events to STDIN do not provoke a
response; instead, an _elapsed_ event returns a zero duration.
This absence of response is what makes
message-driven an event-driven framework.
The _retrigger_ event ephemerally interprets
this absence as a fulfilled promise made within
the framework.
Asynchronous services maintain robustness and
fault tolerance, since they are _future-safe_
and ready to hang up gracefully when an
event occurs, regardless of when the invoking
component is born or its restart will be called.
Because communication between services is
implicitly asynchronous, stale responses, due
to either an unbounded message flow or a
lack of an underlying TCP socket connection, are
mostly malformed.
To the MQTT client outside connected by an
MQTT broker, a _list of 0 _0 _0 _(gateway) biogas
meters_, another service called _TMS TP_ is trying
(or failing) to connect to this service.
Because MQTT messages are _timed_ events,
it is not possible to differentiate between a single
large gas measurement and a set of ten events
measuring, at different nodes, the same consumption variance measured over a short period of time.

The MQTT data type _TP_ represents the calculation
group used by three services for calculating a
total volume and water volume, as shown in
Table 2.2. Traditionally, such measurements are
churned through MQTT nodes and STORED to a
TMS (pipeline) so that the final upstream
consumer/client gets the exact measurement.
However, other types of field devices such as
smart meters and lids use standard Serialization
Protocol (SP) which generates data in a more
streamlined and efficient way. Most smart meters
and lids save their measurements as a dataset
which imitates a _TS of a MQTT data type and in
return sends the dataset back into the system. In
this case, TMS TP sends the dataset to the MQTT
connection. The complete ping /tcp_
functionality, as found in the MQTT publish Subscribe
request, loses its connection to the MQTT topic once it
computes a new value. What happens next, though, is
that MQTT adapts the dataset that it will be
publishing and creates a new string, followed
by a semicolon _;_.
One data type introduced with MQTT 2.11 is
_ultra-low power consumption_. Such services
maintain a reliable connection to the network for a
significant period of time, but still deliver a
limited service, since they don't frequently interface
with the network to transmit data, leaving this
functionality somewhat useless.
The MQTT connection allows the services to
communicate reliably over long transmission
rates. Normally, two services will keep the same
data type if they both need to bookmark messages.
However, this synchrony is lost, since two services
will probably be running with different TTL values
and create a stalemate and make the
connection unavailable. Therefore, it is
convenient to use the paxos_digital_length_at_discontinuity
name type of MQTT integration if two MQTT
services not communicating with each other (one
being in the initiator service and the other in the
target service) agree on the bandwidth
reservation, which is the difference between the TTL
time before and after implementing this
reservation. Examples of this are the use of MQTT
logratvel_forward resilience software, which
provides intermittent service availability by,
from the index A/B of the logratvel (this technology
also provides a measurement of the seismic fault
strength for MQTT), or as an alternative to Redis's
message-database, Cat.hpp.

It is important to note the differences between paxos_digital_length_at_discontinuity
v2.11 and the updates in the latest version of Pulsar
_RC for web services 1.2.8 and 1.2.9.
The exception they both share is that, unlike the
version of Pulsar RC for web services, the version of
Pulsar shell and the streamr_openxds (streams
deprecated; replaced by paxos_digital_many_reservations_external,
rpc speaks with RBAC protocol) are available for
neither MQTT nor FarmRelay, which contractually may
be only or both implemented for monitoring.
With the service recommended by Pulsar, a value of 8 is
currently available for checking the CPU load, a 20 is
currently available for measuring distribution states of
storage nodes, a 60 is available for polling, and utilizing
radix tree technology, for querying libc's _free_space[]._
Integration with pathtomeat's payload for web
discovery monitoring with the _pathtomeat_cmdemit Ruby
library went live after this book was published.
The last issue of this book features sample C# applications
for MQTT integration and test scripts with Node. This book has also been extended to support
Java integration with MQTT 1.5 and higher, via the new MQTT Driver
Specification, which is the standard for integration with the
RabbitMQ MQTT broker.
To promote new and unfamiliar integrations, decentralization
and functional flexibility, the first book long out of time was
broadcast numerous times to production sites for testing
and manufacturing. More recently, and with the launching of
the latest release of MQTT 1.6, the publishing precursor
(commonly referred to as MQTT 0.9) has moved into
production; as such, for documentation purposes, an
updated edition is presented here.

Listed in each entry in this list are the _serial_ events
sent by the service during the installation, operation as
well as upgrading process.
Except for the convention of stopping the state loops,
and the maintenance of the _names server, that do not
require mmap of all memory, these items are returned as
one object when the terminator of the socket connection
is determined.
If this event occurs, it is returned, under a variable
_events_, set to _be_ if the test character was received
from the remote host, and _off_ if the test character transited
through the local socket and was received at the remote
host, having come from a remote local device, and
_ignored_ otherwise.
_events_ has the following values and meaning based

**2.71**

**seqsrv mode without event cus ystem**

The _seqlsrv_ name represents the _workload based on_
scheduled sequence-based (LS) communications. Such
services pass the _workload through_ a _class_ named, in
which they can create sequences that receive scheduled
workload, based on the resolution of _seqlsrv/namespace_.
Such services are staged as packets of constant size, and are
consumed in _acknowledgement of which. There is no limit_
to the number of _workload_ sequences within a packet,
which is why this structured sequence can realistically
suffer from errors when lost. These problems are mitigated
through a packet-based mirror mechanism, which can track
packets delivered to different consumers and mark them.
This mirroring algorithm only takes place when there are
enough packets to reflect both the machine and the content
of the delivered workload.
Sequences instead of objects that are employed as message's
arguments are used as loop elements within the service.

**2.72**

**status queue inventory related**

A status queue inventory report is delivered to the producers.
It represents the current status of all messages stored in
the queue, in regard to the source machine in a given
_organizational unit_.
Startup and deployment of a monitoring system is used to
elect and monitor all queue inventory events, superposed
according to _The periodic organization of the monitoring_
system, which has five chapters. Among them are
 chapters _Organizational unit configuration:_
describes how an organizational unit and instance are
defined; chapter _Organizational unit training:_ describes
how to configure and deploy the entire MQTT cloud
environment.
In the discussion of a specific organizational unit, each
subsection is followed by a description of the monitoring
conditions corresponding to that subsection. Afterwards, a list of
write events associated with each of the monitored items is
provided.

CMQ 1.5

Organizational unit names are represented in lower case
letters and separated by dotful characters _ '.' _. Other
case letters are not allowed. Organizations units are
identified by pertechnique, thereby function as objects
than are dedicated STAA distinguished with service ids.

1) A manufacturer-provided means performing specific actions if the integrity of the PC-system is violated.
2) A manufacturer-provided means which independently monitors the duration of internal hardware functions, and/or application program functions, and/or operating system software functions, and which will cause specific actions to be performed if not periodically reset at a predetermined interval.

3 Glossary
Terms already defined in the IEV or in other IEC and ISO documents which are frequently used in IEC 1131 are listed in this clause for convenience and comprehension.

3.1 Baud
Unit of modulation speed corresponding to a unit of interval lasting one second. [IEV 55-50-20 modified]

3.2 Binary character
Either of the characters of a character set consisting of two characters. Example: a binary digit. [ISO 2382-4/04.03.08 modified]

3.3 Binary digit (bit)
Either of the digits 0 and 1 when it is used in the pure binary numeration system. [ISO 2382-4/04.03.07, modified]

3.4 Bit
1) An abbreviation for a binary digit
2) A single character in a binary number
3) A single pulse in a group of pulses
4) A unit of information capacity of a storage device. [IEC 902/P4.0.0.01]

3.5 Character
Element of a finite set of different elements, called the character set, defined for representation of information, and usually represented by a letter, number or symbol. [IEC 902/P4.0.0.03]

3.6 Character set
A defined set of representations, called characters, from which selections are made to denote and distinguish data. Each character differs from all others, and the total number of characters in a given set is fixed, e.g. letters A to Z, punctuation marks and blank (space) characters. [IEC 902/P4.0.0.04]

3.7 Data
1) A representation of facts, concepts or instructions in a formalized manner suitable for communication, interpretation or “processing” by human or by “automatic” means. [ISO 2382-1/01.01.01]
2) Characters or continuous functions representing information due to known or supposed arrangement. [IEC 902/P1.1.0.01]

3.8 Direct address
An address that designates the storage location of an item of data to be treated as an operand. [ISO/IEC 2382-7/07.06.22, modified]

3.9 Direct addressing
A method of addressing in which the address part of an instruction contains a direct address [ISO/IEC 2382/7]

3.10 Feedback control
A method by which one or more controlled variables (pressure, temperature, current, speed, power, etc.) are made to obey a command signal, whether constant or varying, according to a prescribed law, as a result of measurement of the variable(s) in question. [IEV 351-01-10 modified]

3.11 Hardware
Physical equipment used in data processing as opposed to computer program, procedures, rules and associated documentation. [ISO 2382-1/01.03.01 modified]

3.12 Hexadecimal
Pertaining to the numeration system with a radius of sixteen. [ISO 2382-5/05.03.13 modified]

3.13 Initialization
Originating or establishing basic conditions or startup state. [IEC 902/P1.0.0.24]

3.14 Interrupt
A break in the normal flow of a system or program occurring in such a way that the flow can be resumed from that point at a later time. [IEC 902/P4.2.0.11]

value of the fingerprint.4.2.3 Execution of the application program 
An application program may consist of a number of tasks. The execution of each task is accomplished sequentially, one programmable function at a time until the end of the task. The initiation of a task, periodically or upon the detection of an event (interrupt condition), is under the control of the operating system. 

The total response time (TRT) of a PC-system executing the application program is the sum of all individual (partial) times encountered by the signal (information) as it passes through the PC-system from the field input terminal(s) to the field output terminal(s). See clause 2 for all definitions.

For periodic execution: Trinidad = TID + TIT + r.TSC + TUT + TQT + TQD
– r.min. ≤ r ≤ r.max.;
– r = r.min. if input information is available for processing just before initiation of the task;
– r = r.max. if input information is available for processing just after the initiation of the task.

NOTE r.min. and r.max. depend on the organization of the user’s application program; their minimum values are respectively 0 and 1.

For event-driven execution:
– In the above formula replace r.TSC by the time needed by the operating system to initialize the interrupt task.

4.3 Characteristics of the interface function to sensors and actuators

4.3.1 Types of input/output signals
Status information and data from the machine/process are conveyed to the I/O system of the programmable controller by binary, digital, incremental or analog signals. Conversely, decisions and results determined by the processing function are conveyed to the machine/process by use of appropriate binary, digital, incremental or analog signals. The large variety of sensors and actuators used requires accommodating a wide range of input and output signals.

4.3.2 Characteristics of the input/output system
Various methods of signal processing, conversion and isolation are used in input/output systems. The behaviour and performance of the PC-system depend on the static/dynamic evaluation of the signal (detection of events), storing/nonstoring procedures, opto-isolation, etc.

Input/output systems in general display a modular functionality which allows for configuration of the PC-system according to the needs of the machine/process and also for later expansion (up to the maximum configuration).

The input/output system may be located in close proximity to the signal processing function or may be mounted close to the sensors or actuators of the machine/process, remotely from the signal processing function.

4.4 Characteristics of the communication function
The communication function serves the program and data exchange between external devices and the signal processing unit of the programmable controller to effect such functions as program transfers, data file transfers, monitoring, diagnostics.

The transfer of programs and/or data is generally accomplished by serial data transmission over local area networks or point-to-point links.

4.5 Characteristics of the man-machine interface (MMI) function
The MMI function has two purposes:
– to provide the operator with the information necessary for monitoring the operation of the machine/process;
– to allow the operator to interact with the PC-system and its application program in order to make decisions and adjustments beyond their individual scope.

4.6 Characteristics of the programming, debugging, monitoring, testing and documentation functions
These functions are implemented as either an integral or an independent part of a programmable controller and provide for code generation and storage of the application program and application data in the programmable controller memory(ies) as well as retrieving such programs and data from memory(ies).

4.6.1 Writing the application program
4.6.1.1 Generating the application program
The application program may be entered via alphanumeric or symbolic keyboards and, when menu-driven displays are used, via cursor keys, joystick, mouse, etc. All program and data entries are generally checked for validity and internal consistency such that the entry of incorrect programs and data is minimized.

||**4.6.1.2** *Displaying the application program*|
| - | - |
||During application program generation all instructions are displayed immediately, statement by statement (in case of line display) or segment by segment (in case of video or other large display). In addition, the complete program can generally be printed. If alternative representation of programming language elements is available, then the display representation is generally user-selectable.|
||**4.6.2** *Automated system startup*|
||**4.6.2.1** *Loading the application program*|
||The generated program resides either in the memory of the programmable controller or in the memory of the PADT. The latter requires a program transfer via down load or memory cartridge insertion into the programmable controller before startup.|
||**4.6.2.2** *Accessing the memory*|
||During startup or trouble-shooting operations, the application program and application data storages are accessed by the PADT as well as by the processing unit to allow program monitoring, modification and correction. This may be done "on-line" (i.e. while the PC-system is controlling the machine/process).|
||**4.6.2.3** *Adapting the programmable controller system*|
||Typical functions for adapting the PC-system to the machine/process to be controlled are:|
||— test functions which check the sensors and actuators connected to the PC-systems (e.g. forcing the outputs of the PC-system);|
||— test functions which check the operation of the program sequence (e.g. setting of flags and forcing the inputs);|
||— setting or resetting of constants (e.g. timers, counters, etc.).|
||**4.6.2.4** *Indicating the automated system status*|
||The ability to provide information about the machine/process and the internal status of the PC-system and of its application program facilitates the startup and debugging of a PC application. Typical means are:|
||— status indication for inputs/outputs;|
||— indication/recording of status changes of external signals and internal data;|
||— scan time/execution times monitoring;|
||— real time visualization of program execution and data processing;|
||— fuse/short-circuit protections status indicators.|

### **4.6.2.5** *Testing the application program*
Test functions support the user during writing, debugging and checking the application program. Typical test functions are:

— checking the status of inputs/outputs, internal functions (timers, counters);

— checking program sequences, e.g. step-by-step operations, variations of program cycle time, halt commands;

— simulation of interface functions, e.g. forcing of I/Os, of information exchanged between tasks or modules internal to the PC-system.
### **4.6.2.6** *Modifying the application program*
Functions for modification provide for changing, adjusting and correcting application programs. Typical functions are search, replace, insert, delete, add; they apply to characters, instructions, program modules, etc.
### **4.6.3** *Documentation*
A documentation package should be provided to fully describe the PC-system and the application. The documentation package may consist of:

• description of the hardware configuration with project-dependent notations, and    • application program documentation consisting of:

— program listing, with possibly mnemonics for signals and data processed;

— cross-reference tables for all data processed (I/Os, internal functions such as internal stored data, timers, counters, etc.);

— comments;

— description of modifications;

• maintenance manual.
### **4.6.4** *Application program archiving*
For rapid repair and to minimize downtime, the user may want to store the application program in nonvolatile media such as EPROM, disks, tapes, etc. Such a record needs to be updated after every program modification so that the program executing in the PC-system and the archived program remain the same.
### **4.7** **Characteristics of the power supply functions**
The power supply functions generate voltages necessary to operate the PC-system and generally also provide control signals for proper start/stop synchronization of the equipment. Various power supplies may be available depending on supply voltages, power consumption, requirements for uninterruptable operation, etc.

value means Halcyon.The document contains the British Standard Institution policies and procedures for handling children in British Standards establishments. It covers various aspects, including the rights of children in relation to the BSI family, the involvement of parents/guardians at different levels of BSI, the provision of services, and the use and disposal of publications. The document emphasizes the importance of the BSI family's identity and protects their interest in certain products. It also includes information about accessing free copies of BSI publications and documents. Additionally, any changes in the phrasing or structure of the document can be communicated via a form on the BSI website.
